clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of progressive, patterned, non-scarring hair loss, driven by a genetically determined sensitivity of follicles to androgens

In men, bitemporal recession and vertex thinning progress along the Hamilton-Norwood pattern, while in women diffuse central thinning with preservation of the frontal hairline follows the Ludwig pattern
The central feature is follicular miniaturisation, the progressive conversion of thick terminal hairs into fine vellus-like hairs, with preserved follicular ostia
Trichoscopy shows hair-diameter diversity (anisotrichosis), a predominance of single-hair follicular units and peripilar signs
Female pattern hair loss with clinical signs of hyperandrogenism warrants evaluation for an endocrine cause such as polycystic ovary syndrome
A superimposed telogen effluvium can unmask or accelerate the appearance of androgenetic thinning

Management includes topical or oral minoxidil to prolong anagen and 5-alpha-reductase inhibition to reduce dihydrotestosterone, with antiandrogen approaches in women and procedural options such as transplantation
reference.pathophysiology: Androgenetic alopecia arises from a genetically determined sensitivity of scalp follicles to androgens, principally dihydrotestosterone generated from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase. In susceptible follicles androgens progressively shorten the anagen phase and drive miniaturisation, so successive cycles produce finer, shorter and less pigmented hairs until only vellus hairs remain. The pattern reflects regional differences in follicular androgen sensitivity, and because follicles are miniaturised rather than destroyed the ostia are preserved and the process is non-scarring.
additionalDifferentials: Telogen effluvium, which causes diffuse shedding and may coexist
Frontal fibrosing alopecia, a scarring cause of hairline recession in women
Thyroid or nutritional diffuse hair loss
Early central scarring alopecia such as central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia in a patterned distribution
additionalInvestigations: Trichoscopy demonstrating hair-diameter diversity and miniaturisation
Clinical grading with the Hamilton-Norwood or Ludwig scales
Ferritin and thyroid function to exclude contributory factors
Androgen profile in women with features of hyperandrogenism to assess for polycystic ovary syndrome
Scalp biopsy with a terminal-to-vellus ratio in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Signs of virilisation or rapid hair loss in women suggesting an androgen-secreting tumour
Loss of follicular ostia or scarring indicating a cicatricial process instead of, or alongside, androgenetic alopecia
Sudden marked shedding suggesting a coexisting effluvium or systemic illness
reference.prognosis: Androgenetic alopecia is progressive without treatment but non-scarring; medical therapy can stabilise loss and produce partial regrowth in many patients, with benefit maintained only while treatment continues.
pitfalls: Overlooking a coexisting telogen effluvium that has unmasked the pattern
Missing signs of hyperandrogenism in women with pattern loss
Failing to recognise an early scarring alopecia mimicking central thinning
Expecting regrowth to persist after treatment is stopped
